newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - ERGO VERSICHERUNGS.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - ERGO VERSICHERUNGS.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN

Munich Re has finally gone ahead with the long-expected consolidation of its domestic primary insurance interests. The creation of Ergo Versicherungsgruppe AG, based in Duesseldorf, brings together Victoria, Hamburg-Mannheimer HM and DKV Deutsche Krankenversicherung. Victoria and HM will be merged to form Ergo, while health market leader DKV will become a subsidiary of that holding, as will the Victoria and Hamburg-Mannheimer operating companies. This includes Victoria's DAS subsidiary. The four brand names are to be kept intact.

The incorporation of Victoria brings to an end the long-running speculation over that company's future. Munich Re has until now directly owned 18.2 percent of Victoria, plus 5.3 percent held indirectly. It obviously reached agreement with the other Victoria shareholders - among them a number of insurers and reinsurers - on the deal. They will not get any cash, but shares in the new Ergo Holding, of which Munich Re will hold some 55 to 60 percent, depending on the detailed evaluation.
Thus, in a remarkable development, Munich Re gains full control over Victoria without paying a single penny.

The new Munich Re primary insurance group will have premium income of 21 billion marks, making it easily the number two in the German market after Allianz which had 1996 gross income of 38 billion marks in its home market.

Munich Re was under immense pressure to rearrange its domestic primary interests. The hotchpotch of companies working independently of each other, without real synergy, was no longer sustainable in the deregulated German market. The sales force of DKV, for example, is passing its non-life business on to Allianz, while Allianz has already switched all health business to its own insurer Vereinte. The number of contracts per insured that remained in the Munich Re-led group was far below that achieved by Allianz.

The new grouping will have sufficient muscle to expand further on an international scale - Victoria and its DAS subsidiary are already among the few German insurers with sizeable international presence.

Both in Germany and in Europe, Munich Re will have to explain to its customers, the primary companies, why they should cede business to a reinsurer which, on the direct level, is one of their main competitors.

No doubt, Munich Re's rivals, notably Swiss Re, will continue to attack using that angle. Munich Re is very much aware of this problem. For that reason it has waited so long with the move to set up a holding structure. Its main argument is that the presence in the primary market improves the risk balance and thus provides additional security for its reinsurance customers.

The deal also raises questions about the relationship of the two sister companies in Munich's Koeniginstrasse, Allianz and Munich Re. They are linked via a 25 percent cross-shareholding and via a quota ceded by Allianz to Munich Re. Munich Re also owns close to 50 percent of Allianz Life.

The formation of Ergo was, no doubt, discussed with Allianz. Although there will be competition between the two in the field, it would be wrong to believe that they will now fall out. They will continue to act ndependently of each other, but with a broad understanding of the way the German market should develop.

Still open in the German market rationalisation process is the future of the Aachen Munich group - where Allianz is certain to keep some form of decisive influence. No doubt, the creation of Ergo will speed up a settlement of that question, too.
And finally, Deutsche Bank, which is watching consolidation in the insurance scene with growing uneasiness, might feel obliged to make a move itself soon - probably involving Nuernberger and Gerling.
